+            "INSERT INTO t\nVALUES (17)\n-- comment\n;"
+            "INSERT INTO t VALUES (29);SELECT v FROM t ORDER BY v;",
+            [[], [], [], [(17,), (29,)]],
+        ),
+        (
+            "CREATE TABLE t (v INTEGER);INSERT INTO t VALUES (17), (29);\n"
+            "DELETE FROM t\nWHERE v = 17\n-- comment\n;"
+            "DELETE FROM t WHERE v = 29;SELECT v FROM t;",
+            [[], [], [], [], []],
+        ),
+    ],
+    ids=["select", "insert", "delete"],
+)
+def test__rules__CV06_newline_preserves_execution(
+    sql: str, expected: list[list[tuple[int, ...]]], dialect: str
+) -> None:
+    """Moving a terminator must not extend a line comment over the next SQL."""
+    config = FluffConfig(
+        configs={"rules": {"convention.terminator": {"multiline_newline": True}}},
+        overrides={"dialect": dialect, "rules": "CV06", "templater": "raw"},
+    )
+    linter = Linter(config=config)
+    fixed = linter.lint_string(sql, fix=True).fix_string()[0]
+
+    assert not linter.parse_string(fixed).violations
+    assert not linter.lint_string(fixed).violations
+    assert linter.lint_string(fixed, fix=True).fix_string()[0] == fixed
+
+    # Both dialect configurations use the same SQLite engine. These flat,
+    # trigger-free statements need no external database or real data.
+    for script in (sql, fixed):
+        with closing(sqlite3.connect(":memory:")) as connection:
+            results = []
+            statement = ""
+            for char in script:
+                statement += char
+                if sqlite3.complete_statement(statement):
+                    results.append(connection.execute(statement).fetchall())
+                    statement = ""
+            assert results == expected

problem_statement.title: CV06 multiline_newline fix comments out the following statement
problem_statement.body:
### Search before asking

This is the separate newline-path follow-up to #8810, coordinated in https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues/8810#issuecomment-6314588593. #8811 intentionally handles only `_handle_semicolon_same_line()`; this issue is not a regression attributed to that PR.

### What Happened

With `multiline_newline = True`, moving a multiline statement's semicolon ahead of a standalone line comment can delete the newline that terminates that comment. The following statement becomes comment text.

### Expected Behaviour

Formatting must preserve both statements and their execution results.

### Observed Behaviour

Input:

```sql
SELECT
1
-- c
;SELECT 2;
```

CV06 output:

```sql
SELECT
1
;
-- cSELECT 2;
```

The output still parses, passes CV06, and is unchanged by another fix. An equivalent synthetic INSERT example leaves only the first of two rows in a fresh in-memory SQLite database. A DELETE example also changes the final row set.

### How to reproduce

Save the input as `example.sql` and the configuration below as `.sqlfluff`, then run:

```sh
sqlfluff fix --rules CV06 example.sql
sqlfluff lint --rules CV06 example.sql
```

### Dialect

Reproduced with SQLFluff's ANSI and SQLite dialect configurations. Execution checks use SQLite only.

### Version

SQLFluff 4.4.0, Python 3.12. Also reproduced from current main `ad1231eab8ad9951e186f3a695e8e9abc586300d` with the Python parser and raw templater. The existing 62 CV06 YAML cases pass on that main baseline. This is not an execution test of #8811's head.

### Configuration

```ini
[sqlfluff]
dialect = sqlite
templater = raw
rules = CV06
processes = 1
use_rust_parser = False

[sqlfluff:rules:convention.terminator]
multiline_newline = True
```

### Are you willing to work on and submit a PR to address the issue?

Yes. I am preparing a narrowly scoped newline-path fix and regression tests, leaving the same-line and nested-statement work to their existing PRs.

### Code of Conduct

I will follow the project's Code of Conduct.

### Validation disclosure

Investigation and this report are AI-assisted. Synthetic execution checks and a separately written probe verified the statement/result loss; no real data or production systems were used.

problem_statement.title: Use zoneinfo / backports.zoneinfo for time zones instead of dateutil.tz?
problem_statement.body:
[PEP 615](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0615/) introduces a new `zoneinfo` module into the standard library starting in Python 3.9. A [backport to Python 3.6 is also available](https://github.com/pganssle/zoneinfo) as `backports.zoneinfo`.

I don't think any support for `pytz` or `dateutil.tz` zones needs to be dropped, but as was done in #10443, I think we can start using it as the default time zone provider.

**Upsides**:
The biggest upside to `zoneinfo` is that it is much faster than `dateutil` (and also faster than `pytz`). `dateutil` is already a dependency for other reasons, so the fact that eventually relying on `zoneinfo` will not require a third-party dependency is more or less moot in this case. `zoneinfo` also has some nicer properties around where it searches for time zones, which is configurable in several ways. This will hopefully also be mooted in `dateutil >= 3.0`, since I plan to refactor `dateutil` to use essentially the same search path as `zoneinfo` when possible.

Additionally, `zoneinfo` currently supports Version 2 TZif files (including dates after 2038), whereas `dateutil` only uses the Version 1 subset. This will hopefully change in a future version of `dateutil` as well.

**Downsides**:
The downsides of switching to `backports.zoneinfo` is that (in Python <3.9) it will add a new dependency, and specifically one that is in a namespace package (`backports.`) and has a C extension. This shouldn't be a big deal considering how many of `matplotlib`'s dependencies have C extensions (this one is particularly easy to build), but it is not uncommon for this sort of thing to add complications. You would also likely want a dependency on `tzdata` as well (though this will not be new because in `dateutil >= 3.0`, `dateutil` will be adding a dependency on that package).

On earlier versions of Python, it also brings in a dependency on `importlib_resources` (which itself depends on `importlib_metadata` and `zipp`). On newer versions of Python, these are in the standard library.

The last downside is that this introduces a semantic change you'd want to think about. Right now, [`tz.gettz()` is used](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/blob/793c6b05381231371267b44b107726f3878e14f2/lib/matplotlib/dates.py#L188-L193), and I believe the assumption is that you'd set your time zone to an IANA zone (since previously it was calling `pytz.timezone`), but `dateutil.tz.gettz` actually accepts a few other types of time zones, like POSIX TZ string formats like `EST5EDT` and such, plus it has the (unfortunate, in my mind) behavior that if it cannot find a time zone, it will return `None`, whereas `ZoneInfo("Amreica/New_York")` will raise an exception. We can pretty easily keep that behavior if desired.

**Summary**

The case for dropping `dateutil` in favor of `zoneinfo` is a lot less clear than the case for dropping `pytz` for `dateutil` was, because on >Python 3.9, this *introduces* rather than removes new dependencies. However, the case for using `zoneinfo` will get a lot stronger as more and more people adopt Python 3.9; it might not be a bad thing to get ahead of the curve there.

Another option might be adding this as an optional "extras" dependency, so that first you try `zoneinfo`, then `backports.zoneinfo` and if neither of those exists, use `dateutil.tz`.

problem_statement.title: Restricting S3 Purge queue to once every 60 seconds is very restrictive
problem_statement.body:
Related Issue #10233
Related PR #10234

IMO this implementation is problematic for a tool being used in local development and at least in my case CI! I call purge_queue 3 times in my integration tests but the whole suite run takes < 2 mins with those calls being very close together.  So it will never pass on Moto 5.2.4

A preferred implementation in my opinion would allow for opt-out behaviour via configuration.  There is prior art in the codebase [MOTO_ALLOW_NONEXISTENT_REGION](https://github.com/getmoto/moto/blob/b2e1636ac8a3093120eb3575659c902c57853a2b/moto/settings.py#L101) which defaults to false

or (MOTO_S3_ALLOW_CROSSACCOUNT_ACCESS)[https://github.com/getmoto/moto/blob/b2e1636ac8a3093120eb3575659c902c57853a2b/moto/settings.py#L83] which defaults to true.  You can see example usage of this at https://github.com/getmoto/moto/blob/b2e1636ac8a3093120eb3575659c902c57853a2b/moto/s3/models.py#L2024

The purge queue method wouldn't change much, perhaps

```
    def purge_queue(self, queue_name: str) -> None:
        queue = self.get_queue(queue_name)
        now = unix_time()
        if sqs_enforce_strict_queue_purge_behaviour() and queue.last_purged_at is not None and now - queue.last_purged_at < 60:
            raise PurgeQueueInProgress(queue.name)
        queue.last_purged_at = now
        queue._messages = []
        queue._pending_messages = set()
```

Would a PR to such effect be tolerated?

problem_statement.title: pdm outdated lists packages whose installed version is newer than the index
problem_statement.body:
`pdm outdated` lists a package as outdated when the installed version is newer than the latest version it finds on the index, and shows the older version under "Latest". With `requests==2.19.1` installed and an index that only has `requests-2.19.0`:

```
$ pdm outdated
+--------------------------------------------------+
| Package  | Groups  | Installed | Pinned | Latest |
|----------+---------+-----------+--------+--------|
| requests | default | 2.19.1    | 2.19.1 | 2.19.0 |
+--------------------------------------------------+
```

This shows up whenever the installed version isn't something the index offers as its best match: a private index that lags behind, a local or dev build, or a pre-release when the finder isn't picking pre-releases.

The filter in `outdated.py` keeps a package when `latest_version != installed_version`, comparing the version strings, so an older "latest" counts as outdated too.

problem_statement.title: is_quantum_channel returns False for channels whose input and output dimensions differ
problem_statement.body:
## Before reporting this bug:
- [x] Verify there is not an existing issue for it already
- [x] You are using the latest version of `toqito` with a Python version `>=3.12`

## Describe the bug
`is_quantum_channel` returns `False` for valid channels whenever the input and output dimensions differ. This happens even when the channel is given as Kraus operators, where the dimensions are unambiguous.

When `phi` is a list, `is_quantum_channel` first converts it with `kraus_to_choi` and then calls `is_trace_preserving` on the Choi matrix without `dim`. `is_trace_preserving` then has to assume two equal subsystems, which raises a `ValueError` for e.g. a 6x6 Choi matrix (qubit to qutrit), and that error is caught and returned as `False`. Calling `is_completely_positive` and `is_trace_preserving` directly on the same Kraus operators gives `True` for both.

For a Choi matrix there is currently no way to pass the dimensions, since `is_quantum_channel` doesn't take a `dim` argument.

This also affects `channel_relative_entropy` and `channel_measured_relative_entropy`. Both take `in_dim` and compute `out_dim = n // in_dim`, but they validate `channel_1` with `is_quantum_channel(channel_1)`, so any channel with `in_dim != out_dim` is rejected.

## To Reproduce
```python
import numpy as np
from toqito.channel_ops import kraus_to_choi
from toqito.channel_props import is_completely_positive, is_quantum_channel, is_trace_preserving

# Embedding a qubit into a qutrit: V^* V = I_2, so rho -> V rho V^* is a valid channel.
V = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [0, 0]])
print(is_completely_positive([V]))  # True
print(is_trace_preserving([V]))     # True
print(is_quantum_channel([V]))      # False (expected True)

# Partial trace over the first qubit of a two-qubit system, Kraus operators <i| (x) I_2.
K = [np.kron(np.eye(2)[[i]], np.eye(2)) for i in range(2)]
print(is_quantum_channel(K))        # False (expected True)
```

And for the relative entropy:

```python
from toqito.channel_metrics import channel_relative_entropy

J1 = kraus_to_choi([V])
J2 = (J1 + np.kron(np.eye(2), np.eye(3) / 3)) / 2
channel_relative_entropy(J1, J2, in_dim=2)
# ValueError: Channel relative entropy is only defined if channel_1 is a quantum channel.
```

## Expected behavior
Both channels above should be reported as quantum channels. A possible fix:

- pass Kraus operators straight to `is_completely_positive` and `is_trace_preserving` (both already handle them) instead of converting to a Choi matrix first,
- add an optional `dim` argument to `is_quantum_channel` that is forwarded to `is_trace_preserving` for Choi matrices, and
- have the two relative entropy functions pass `dim=[in_dim, n // in_dim]`.

With that change, `channel_measured_relative_entropy` on the example above gives 0.538997, which matches -ln(7/12). (For a maximally entangled input, the output of the first channel is pure and is an eigenvector of the second channel's output with eigenvalue 1/2 + 1/12.)

I have a fix with tests ready and will open a PR.

issue_title: support for generic type aliases used for annotations

gold_patch:
diff --git a/cyclopts/annotations.py b/cyclopts/annotations.py
index e1c145cb..2dd50701 100644
--- a/cyclopts/annotations.py
+++ b/cyclopts/annotations.py
@@ -289,9 +289,25 @@ def resolve_new_type(type_: Any) -> type:
 
 
 def resolve_type_alias(type_: Any) -> Any:
-    """Resolve TypeAliasType (Python 3.12+ 'type' statement) to its underlying type."""
-    if TypeAliasType is not None and isinstance(type_, TypeAliasType):
+    """Resolve TypeAliasType (Python 3.12+ 'type' statement) to its underlying type.
+
+    A subscripted generic alias (``type Alias[T] = ...`` used as ``Alias[int]``) resolves
+    to its value with the type arguments substituted.
+    """
+    if TypeAliasType is None:
+        return type_
+    if isinstance(type_, TypeAliasType):
         return type_.__value__
+    origin = get_origin(type_)
+    if isinstance(origin, TypeAliasType):
+        substitutions = dict(zip(origin.__type_params__, get_args(type_), strict=True))
+        value = origin.__value__
+        if value in substitutions:
+            return substitutions[value]
+        parameters = getattr(value, "__parameters__", ())
+        if not parameters:
+            return value
+        return value[tuple(substitutions[p] for p in parameters)]
     return type_

problem_statement.title: support for generic type aliases used for annotations
problem_statement.body:
First of all, thanks for your work!

Please check the example snippet below. It has two commands `base` and `tvar` which are intended to behave the same. But `base` uses pair of exact type aliases whereas `tvar` uses generic type aliases:

Example:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Annotated
from cyclopts import App, Parameter


app = App()


@dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True)
class Upper:
    upper: bool = False


@dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True)
class Lower:
    lower: bool = False


type UpperOpts = Annotated[Upper, Parameter(name='*')]
type LowerOpts = Annotated[Lower, Parameter(name='*')]


@app.command
def base(
    *,
    upper: UpperOpts = Upper(),
    lower: LowerOpts = Lower(),
) -> None:
    print(upper.upper, lower.lower)


type Opts[OptsT] = Annotated[OptsT, Parameter(name='*')]


@app.command
def tvar(
    *,
    upper: Opts[Upper] = Upper(),
    lower: Opts[Lower] = Lower(),
):
    print(upper.upper, lower.lower)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    app()
```

```
$ python ./example.py base --upper --lower
$ python ./example.py tvar --upper --lower
```

Expected result:

Both commands behave the same.

Observed result:

Generic type alias version does not work correctly:

```
Command "tvar" parameter --upper requires an argument.
```

issue_title: [Bug]: QuickPlot does not follow matplotlib's colour cycle

index c99486239e..65eb403978 100644
--- a/CHANGELOG.md
+++ b/CHANGELOG.md
@@ -30,6 +30,7 @@
 - Fixed copying a function without simplification, as `ParameterValues` does for a parameter set loaded with `Serialise.load_parameters`, returning a generic `pybamm.Function`: `pybamm.exp` and the other specific functions lost their class, and an `Arcsinh2` copy could not be evaluated. ([#5954](https://github.com/pybamm-team/PyBaMM/pull/5954))
 - `RegPower` now evaluates the same operations in `evaluate` and CasADi, taking a literal exponent of 0.5 or 2 as square roots, so they agree bitwise; CasADi used a `hypot` form. With `delta=0`, `evaluate` and the Jacobian use `base ** exponent`, as CasADi did. ([#5955](https://github.com/pybamm-team/PyBaMM/pull/5955))
 - CasADi linear and `pchip` interpolants on a uniform grid now find a point's segment by binary search. The `"exact"` lookup could pick the neighbouring segment at or one ulp beside a knot, giving the Jacobian that segment's slope. ([#5955](https://github.com/pybamm-team/PyBaMM/pull/5955))
+- `QuickPlot`, and so `Simulation.plot`, now uses matplotlib's color cycle (`axes.prop_cycle`) for default colors when a style sheet or rcParams changes it; otherwise it keeps its red, blue, black, green, magenta and cyan colors. ([#5953](https://github.com/pybamm-team/PyBaMM/pull/5953))

problem_statement.title: [Bug]: QuickPlot does not follow matplotlib's colour cycle
problem_statement.body:
### PyBaMM Version

26.10

### Python Version

3.14

### Describe the bug

PyBaMM's QuickPlot hardcodes the colour cycle, which can't be overwritten through matplotlib, despite what QuickPlot's docstring says

```
    colors : list of str, optional
        The colors to loop over when plotting. Defaults to None, in which case the default color loop defined by matplotlib style sheet or rcParams is used.
```


### Steps to Reproduce

```python
import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pybamm
from cycler import cycler

# A minimal model and solution
model = pybamm.BaseModel()
x = pybamm.Variable("x")
model.rhs = {x: -x}
model.initial_conditions = {x: 1}
model.variables = {"x": x}
solution = pybamm.Simulation(model).solve([0, 1])

# The docstring says the default colours follow matplotlib's colour cycle
plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"] = cycler(color=["#123456", "#abcdef"])
quick_plot = pybamm.QuickPlot(solution, ["x"])
print("matplotlib cycle:", plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"].by_key()["color"])
print("QuickPlot colours:", list(quick_plot.colors))

# And the line actually drawn
quick_plot.plot(0.5)
line = quick_plot.plots[("x",)][0][0]
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
matplotlib cycle: ['#123456', '#abcdef']
QuickPlot colours: ['r', 'b', 'k', 'g', 'm', 'c']
colour of the plotted line: r
```

problem_statement.title: Bug: ack_policy is ignored when an error occurs before the handler call
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**
`_AcknowledgementMiddleware` sets `self.message` only in `consume_scope`. If an error
happens earlier — in a middleware `on_receive`, a custom parser, a filter, or no
suitable handler is found — `__aexit__` runs with `self.message is None`, and
`ack/nack/reject` silently do nothing. The message is never settled.

This also means `raise AckMessage()/RejectMessage()` from `on_receive` or a parser is
suppressed, but no ack/reject is sent. And with `AckPolicy.ACK_FIRST` (where it is
handled by this middleware, e.g. Redis Streams) such messages are never acked.

**How to reproduce**
```python
from faststream import AckPolicy, BaseMiddleware, FastStream
from faststream.rabbit import RabbitBroker

class FailingMiddleware(BaseMiddleware):
    async def on_receive(self) -> None:
        raise ValueError("boom")

broker = RabbitBroker(middlewares=[FailingMiddleware])
app = FastStream(broker)

@broker.subscriber("test", ack_policy=AckPolicy.REJECT_ON_ERROR)
async def handler(body): ...
```
Run it, publish any message to `test`, then check
`rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages_unacknowledged`.

**Expected behavior**
The message is rejected according to `ack_policy`.

**Observed behavior**
The message stays `Unacked` until the channel closes. Once `prefetch_count` such
messages accumulate, the consumer stops receiving new ones.

**Additional context**
Proposed fix: when `self.message is None`, lazily build it with the subscriber's
default (non-custom) parser in `_AcknowledgementMiddleware` (inside 
`__ack/__nack/__reject`, so suppressed exceptions and `ACK_FIRST` are covered too).

I would like to implement it myself :)

 In `optimize_mga`, the bound on total system cost is specified as a relative increase over the cost-optimum; the relative increase is called _slack_. Denote the slack as $\varepsilon$, as is common in the literature, and let $c$ be the total system cost objective function and $c^*$ its optimal value. Then the near-optimality constraint added in `optimize_mga` is $c \leq (1 + \varepsilon) \cdot c^*$. Typical values found in the literature range from about 2% to 20%, with 5% being a common starting value for exploration.
 
+The budget is based on [`n.statistics.system_cost()`][pypsa.statistics.StatisticsAccessor.system_cost], which includes investment costs, fixed operation and maintenance costs, and operational costs of both extendable and non-extendable assets.
+
+Fixed costs contribute to both sides of the budget. Although they do not change the cost-optimal solution, they count toward total system cost and therefore affect the absolute cost increase permitted by the relative slack. Consequently, `n.objective`, which may omit or subtract fixed costs, should not be used directly as the total system cost.

problem_statement.title: MGA budget with investment periods multiplies the cost statistics by the period weight a second time
problem_statement.body:
> [!NOTE]
> This issue was drafted by AI.

### Version Checks (indicate both or one)

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest [release](https://github.com/pypsa/pypsa/releases) of PyPSA (1.3.0).
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the current [`master`](https://github.com/pypsa/pypsa/tree/master) branch of PyPSA (51986084).

### Issue Description

`optimize_mga(..., multi_investment_periods=True)` and `optimize_mga_in_direction(..., multi_investment_periods=True)` build the budget row `objective + fixed_cost <= (1 + slack) * optimal_cost`. With investment periods, `_add_near_opt_constraint` multiplies `capex`, `opex` and `installed_capex` by `investment_period_weightings.objective`. Since #1646 (in v1.2.0), these statistics already carry that weight. So the budget counts the period weight twice.

The budget is then too loose by a factor near the period weight. In the example, the period weights are 10 and 5. The optimal total cost is 630. With `slack=0.05`, the MGA solution may cost 661.5. PyPSA allows 4192.5, which is 6.65 times the optimum. No error or warning is raised.

### Reproducible Example

Run with `uv run --script mre.py`.

```python
# /// script
# dependencies = ["pypsa @ git+https://github.com/PyPSA/PyPSA@51986084bfb68d38e5b64021649cb339448112cb", "highspy"]
# ///
import pandas as pd
import pypsa

n = pypsa.Network()
n.set_snapshots(pd.MultiIndex.from_product([[2020, 2030], [0]]))
n.investment_periods = [2020, 2030]
n.investment_period_weightings.loc[:, "objective"] = [10.0, 5.0]
n.add("Bus", "b")
n.add("Generator", "g", bus="b", p_nom_extendable=True, capital_cost=2, marginal_cost=1)
n.add("Generator", "h", bus="b", p_nom_extendable=True, capital_cost=3, marginal_cost=1)
n.add("Generator", "old", bus="b", p_nom=3, capital_cost=4, marginal_cost=10)
n.add("Load", "l", bus="b", p_set=10)
n.optimize(multi_investment_periods=True, log_to_console=False)

w = n.investment_period_weightings.objective
capex = n.statistics.capex().sum()
opex = n.statistics.opex().sum()
installed = n.statistics.installed_capex().sum()
print("model objective:", n.objective)
print("capex per period:", capex.to_dict())
print("opex per period:", opex.to_dict())
print("installed_capex per period:", installed.to_dict())
print("total cost, sum of statistics:", (capex + opex).sum())
print("optimal_cost in budget, statistics x w:", ((capex + opex) * w).sum())

n.optimize.optimize_mga(
    multi_investment_periods=True,
    slack=0.05,
    weights={"Generator": {"p_nom": {"g": 1}}},
    log_to_console=False,
)
intended_rhs = 1.05 * (capex + opex).sum() - installed.sum()
print("budget rhs, PyPSA:", float(n.model.constraints["budget"].rhs))
print("budget rhs, statistics without x w:", intended_rhs)
print("MGA p_nom_opt:", n.generators.p_nom_opt.to_dict())
print("total cost after MGA, sum of statistics:", (n.statistics.capex().sum() + n.statistics.opex().sum()).sum())
```

Output (stdout, solver log and warnings removed):

```
model objective: 450.0
capex per period: {2020: 320.0, 2030: 160.0}
opex per period: {2020: 100.0, 2030: 50.0}
installed_capex per period: {2020: 120.0, 2030: 60.0}
total cost, sum of statistics: 630.0
optimal_cost in budget, statistics x w: 5250.0
budget rhs, PyPSA: 4012.5
budget rhs, statistics without x w: 481.5
MGA p_nom_opt: {'g': 0.0, 'h': 76.83333333333333, 'old': 3.0}
total cost after MGA, sum of statistics: 4192.5
```

`n.objective` is 450 because the capital cost of a unit that is not extendable is not in the objective. The fixed capacity `old` costs 180, so the total cost is 630. The statistics give 630, which is correct.

### Expected Behavior

- `optimal_cost` is `(capex + opex).sum()` over all periods: 630.
- `fixed_cost` is `installed_capex.sum()` over all periods: 180.
- The budget row has a right side of `1.05 * 630 - 180 = 481.5`. The MGA solution costs at most 661.5.

Actual: right side 4012.5. The MGA solution costs 4192.5.

### Cause

On 51986084:

- `pypsa/optimization/mga.py:259-263` multiplies the per-period sums of `n.statistics.capex()`, `n.statistics.opex()` and `n.statistics.installed_capex()` by `w = n.investment_period_weightings.objective`.
- `pypsa/statistics/expressions.py:772-774` (`capex`), `:888-890` (`installed_capex`) and `:1712-1714` (`opex`) already multiply each period by `investment_period_weightings["objective"]`.
- #827 added the weight in the MGA budget in 2024, when the statistics were unweighted. #1646 then added the weight in the statistics. The MGA branch was not changed.

### Proposed direction

Remove `* w` in `mga.py:259-263`. Then both branches compute the same sums, and the `if not multi_investment_periods` branch can go. A test with period weights other than 1 would catch a regression.

### Related

- #827 added the period weight in the MGA budget.
- #1646 (closes #1287) added the period weight to the cost statistics.
- #1923 (open) adds the period weight to the `fom` statistic, as #1646 did for `capex` and `opex`. The budget does not read `fom`.
- #1340 (open) changes MGA runs but not the budget weight.

Found while recording PyPSA reference models for [energy-models/mathspec#833](https://github.com/energy-models/mathspec/issues/833).

### Installed Versions

<details>

- pypsa 1.3.0.post1.dev41+g51986084b
- linopy 0.9.1
- highspy 1.15.1
- pandas 3.0.6
- xarray 2026.9.0
- Python 3.13.11

</details>

problem_statement.title: `cookies._read_set_cookie_pairs` swallows subsequent attributes into `Expires` when `Expires` is short (e.g. `Expires=0; Secure`)
problem_statement.body:
### Problem Description

`mitmproxy.net.http.cookies.parse_set_cookie_header` swallows subsequent attributes (such as `Secure` or `HttpOnly`) into the `Expires` attribute value when `Expires` contains three or fewer characters (such as `Expires=0; Secure`).

#### Reproduction

```python
from mitmproxy.net.http import cookies

# Set-Cookie with Expires=0 followed by Secure
parsed = cookies.parse_set_cookie_header("session=abc; Expires=0; Secure; HttpOnly")

# Actual result:
# [('session', 'abc', CookieAttrs[('Expires', '0, Secure'), ('HttpOnly', None)])]
# 'Secure' is missing from the cookie attributes and merged into 'Expires'.

# Expected result:
# [('session', 'abc', CookieAttrs[('Expires', '0'), ('Secure', None), ('HttpOnly', None)])]
# 'Secure' is parsed as a distinct attribute with value None.
```

#### Root Cause

In `mitmproxy/net/http/cookies.py`, `_read_set_cookie_pairs` parses attributes in Set-Cookie headers using delimiters `;,`. When handling `Expires`, the code attempts to handle commas in HTTP date formats (such as RFC 1123 `Wed, 09 Jun 2021...`):

```python
            if lhs.lower() == "expires":
                if len(rhs) <= 3:
                    trail, off = _read_value(s, off + 1, ";,")
                    rhs = rhs + "," + trail
```

1. The check `if len(rhs) <= 3:` does not verify whether the delimiter that terminated `rhs` was actually a comma. If the attribute terminates at a semicolon (`;`) with `len(rhs) <= 3` (e.g., `Expires=0; Secure`), `_read_value` is called with `off + 1`, skipping past the semicolon and consuming the next attribute (`Secure`) into `rhs`.
2. For comma-separated multiple cookies in a single header (e.g., `a=b; expires=0, c=d`), the second cookie `c=d` is consumed into `Expires`.
3. For RFC 850 dates with full weekday names (e.g., `Wednesday, 21-Oct-2026 07:28:00 GMT; path=/`), `len("Wednesday") > 3`, which fails `len(rhs) <= 3` and incorrectly splits the date across the comma into a phantom second cookie.

#### Affected Ranges (Scope)

- Affected inputs: Any `Set-Cookie` header where `Expires` has a short value (`Expires=0`, `Expires=-1`, etc.) followed by other attributes or subsequent cookies, as well as `Set-Cookie` headers using RFC 850 date strings with full weekday names.
- Scope: Narrow to `mitmproxy.net.http.cookies._read_set_cookie_pairs`.
- Severity: Moderate logic / parsing defect; causes silent loss of security attributes (`Secure`, `HttpOnly`) when inspecting or modifying session cookies that use `Expires=0` idioms.

#### Finding Method

Found during code audit of cookie parsing against RFC 6265 and RFC 850 specifications.

#### System Information

```
Mitmproxy: 13.0.0.dev
Commit: 7735597
Python: 3.14.6
Platform: macOS-27.0.1-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O
```

#### Checklist

- [x] This bug affects the latest mitmproxy release.
